nameStory: The word 'chipmunk' comes from the Ojibwe word 'ajidamoo,' meaning 'one who descends trees headlong' - a perfect description of these acrobatic little mammals! Early French traders called them 'chitmunk,' which eventually became our modern 'chipmunk.' The 'eastern' part simply distinguishes this species from the western chipmunks found across the Rocky Mountains.
description: Eastern chipmunks are small, striped ground squirrels about the size of a hamster, typically 8-10 inches long including their fluffy tail. They're easily recognized by their rusty-brown fur marked with five dark stripes running down their back and sides, plus bright white stripes in between. These energetic little mammals have large cheek pouches that can puff out comically when stuffed with seeds and nuts. They're the only chipmunk species found in New England, making identification straightforward once you know what to look for.

idTips.label: Fur
idTips.description: Five distinct dark brown or black stripes run down the back, separated by bright white or cream stripes. The overall fur color is rusty-brown to reddish, with a white belly. The stripes extend from the shoulders to the rump but not onto the tail.

idTips.label: Size & Shape
idTips.description: About 8-10 inches total length with a proportionally shorter, less bushy tail than tree squirrels. Body feels compact and low to the ground, weighing roughly 2-5 ounces - about the weight of a small smartphone.

idTips.label: Behavior
idTips.description: Cheeks bulge dramatically when carrying food, sometimes looking almost comical. Quick, jerky movements with frequent pauses to sit upright and survey surroundings. Often seen scurrying along the ground rather than in trees.

idTips.label: Tracks
idTips.description: Four-toed front feet and five-toed hind feet, each about 1/2 inch long. Tracks show tiny claw marks, and you'll often see them leading to or from small burrow entrances about 2 inches wide.

idTips.label: Sign
idTips.description: Look for small, neat piles of nut shells and acorn caps near rocks or logs. Burrow entrances are clean and round, often hidden under brush piles or stone walls, with no obvious dirt mounds nearby.

idTips.label: Habitat
idTips.description: Prefers areas with both trees for food and rocky or loose soil for burrowing. Often found near stone walls, fallen logs, and brush piles that provide cover and nesting sites.

habitat: Eastern chipmunks thrive in mixed deciduous and coniferous forests throughout New England, especially areas with oak, maple, and beech trees that provide abundant nuts and seeds. They favor locations with rocky outcrops, stone walls, or loose, well-drained soil perfect for their extensive burrow systems. You'll often spot them in suburban areas with mature trees, parks, and wooded neighborhoods where they can find both food sources and suitable denning sites.

seasonality.spring: Chipmunks emerge from winter dormancy in March or April, looking noticeably thinner after months of living off stored fat. This is mating season, so you might hear more chittering calls and see increased activity around burrow sites.
seasonality.summer: Peak activity time when chipmunks are most visible, foraging actively throughout the day. You'll see them with dramatically bulging cheek pouches as they gather and cache food for winter.
seasonality.fall: Frantic preparation mode as they stuff cheek pouches with acorns, nuts, and seeds. Their fur becomes thicker and more vibrant, and they may appear noticeably plumper as they build fat reserves.
seasonality.winter: Unlike true hibernators, chipmunks enter torpor - a lighter sleep where they wake periodically to eat cached food. You might occasionally see tracks in snow during warm spells, but sightings are rare.

funFact: A single chipmunk can gather and store up to 8 pounds of food in their burrow for winter - that's like a 150-pound person stockpiling 2,400 pounds of groceries! Their cheek pouches can stretch to three times the size of their head, allowing them to carry up to 32 beechnuts in a single trip.
confusionNotes: Most commonly confused with red squirrels, but remember 'Stripes Stay Still' - chipmunks have bold stripes and spend more time on the ground, while red squirrels are solid-colored and live primarily in trees. Ground squirrels (not found in New England) would be larger and lack the distinct facial stripes that chipmunks have.
contextualKnowledge: Despite their name suggesting they're closely related to squirrels, chipmunks are actually more closely related to marmots and prairie dogs. Many people don't realize that the familiar cartoon chipmunks Chip and Dale are actually based on western chipmunk species - our eastern chipmunks have slightly different stripe patterns and proportions.
compareHints: Eastern chipmunks are the only chipmunk species in New England, making them unique in their genus here. Compared to their closest relatives in the squirrel family, they're much smaller than gray squirrels (which lack stripes entirely) and have more prominent stripes than the rusty-colored red squirrels. Unlike tree squirrels, chipmunks have internal cheek pouches and are primarily ground-dwelling rather than arboreal.
